keyVerseText: And the priests, Aaron's sons, shall lay the parts, the head, and the fat, in order upon the wood that is on the fire which is upon the altar:
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun פֶּדֶר (peder) derives from an unused root meaning 'to be greasy,' which highlights its fundamental association with fat or suet. This etymological insight deepens the common English gloss of 'fat' by emphasizing not just the substance itself but its oily, rich nature. Understanding peder as 'greasy fat' enriches our grasp of its physical and symbolic qualities in the biblical text.
usageInScripture: The word peder appears three times in Scripture, consistently referring to the fat or suet associated with sacrificial offerings. Its top translations, 'and the fat' (twice) and 'and his fat' (once), show a narrow semantic range focused on the fatty portions of sacrifices. This consistency underscores its specialized use in the cultic context, where the fat holds particular ritual significance.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, peder's emphasis on fat as a distinct and valued part of the offering points to the holiness and dedication required in worship. Fat, being rich and substantial, symbolizes the best and most precious parts given to God, reflecting the believer's call to offer their whole selves in devotion. Recognizing peder as 'greasy fat' also reminds us of the tangible, physical nature of Old Testament sacrifices that prefigure Christ's ultimate offering, who gave Himself fully and richly for our redemption.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 1:8 instructs the priests to lay the parts of the sacrifice, including 'the head, and the fat,' in order upon the wood on the altar's fire. The word peder here highlights the fat as an essential component of the burnt offering, symbolizing the dedication of the choicest portions to God. This detail enriches the verse by showing the care and reverence with which the offering is presented, pointing forward to the perfect sacrifice of Christ, whose offering was wholly pleasing to the Father.
